content: Sea-buckthorn, scientifically known as Hippophae L., belongs to the genus Hippophae within the family Elaeagnaceae. These are deciduous shrubs, and the name sea-buckthorn is hyphenated to distinguish it from buckthorns of the genus Rhamnus in the family Rhamnaceae. It is also referred to as sea buckthorn, seabuckthorn, sandthorn, or seaberry. The plant is recognized by various names in different languages, such as Shaji in Chinese, Duindoorn in Dutch, Tyrni in Finnish, Argousier in French, Sanddorn in German, Olivello Spinoso in Italian, Облепиха (Oblepiha) in Russian, Espino de Mar or Espino Amarillo in Spanish, and Havtorn in Swedish and Danish. Since 2005, sea-buckthorn berries have gained significant recognition in the United States, other developed countries, and the global functional food industry. This is due to their exceptional nutrient content, antioxidant properties, and potential for consumer products, earning them the status of a novel superfruit. Description and Distribution There are six species and 12 subspecies of sea-buckthorn, native to a wide range of regions across Europe and Asia, including China, Mongolia, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Russia, Great Britain, France, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Norway. Approximately 5 million hectares of the world's sea-buckthorn resources are located in China, where the plant is utilized for soil and water conservation. These shrubs typically grow to a height of 5–6 meters, though they can reach up to 18 meters in Central Asia. They thrive in dry, sandy areas and are highly tolerant of salt in both air and soil. However, they require full sunlight for optimal growth and cannot tolerate shade from larger trees. The most widespread species is the common sea-buckthorn (Hippophae rhamnoides), which ranges from the Atlantic coasts of Europe to northwestern China. In Western Europe, it is primarily found along sea coasts, where salt spray prevents competition from larger plants. In Central Asia, it is more common in dry, semi-desert areas where other plants cannot survive. In Central Europe and Asia, it also grows as a subalpine shrub above the tree line in mountains and in sunny areas such as riverbanks. The common sea-buckthorn has dense, stiff, and thorny branches. Its leaves are pale silvery-green, lanceolate, and measure 3–8 cm in length and less than 7 mm in width. The plant is dioecious, meaning male and female plants are separate. Male plants produce brownish flowers that release wind-distributed pollen. Berries and Leaves Female sea-buckthorn plants produce orange berries that are 6–9 mm in diameter, soft, juicy, and exceptionally rich in vitamin C, with an average content of 600 mg per 100 g, and sometimes up to 1500 mg per 100 g. Some varieties are also rich in vitamin A, vitamin E, and oils. These berries serve as an important winter food source for certain bird species, such as fieldfares. The leaves are consumed by the larvae of various moth species, including the coastal race of the ash pug moth, brown-tail, the dun-bar, emperor moth, mottled umber, and Coleophora elaeagnisella. The species Hippophae salicifolia (willow-leaved sea-buckthorn) is restricted to the Himalayas, growing at high altitudes in dry valleys. It differs from H. rhamnoides by having broader (up to 10 mm wide), greener (less silvery) leaves and yellow berries. Another species, Hippophae tibetana (Tibetan sea-buckthorn), grows at even higher altitudes in the alpine zone. It is a low shrub, not exceeding 1 meter in height, with small leaves measuring 1–3 cm in length. Two additional species, Hippophae goniocarpa and Hippophae neurocarpa, have been described in China but are not widely accepted as distinct. Uses Harvesting and Landscaping Harvesting sea-buckthorn berries is challenging due to the dense thorns on the shrubs. A common method involves removing entire branches, which is destructive to the plant and reduces future harvests. The removed branches are frozen, allowing the berries to be easily shaken off. Branches are cut and deep-frozen to −32°C, then slightly defrosted on the surface during berry removal. The berries are later stored at −22°C. A more efficient harvesting method involves using a berry-shaker, developed in Estonia, which minimizes damage to the branches. However, mechanical harvesting leaves up to 50% of the berries in the field and allows harvesting only once every two years, yielding about 25% of the potential crop. During the Cold War, Russian and East German horticulturists developed new varieties with improved nutritional value, larger berries, different ripening times, and branch forms that are easier to harvest. Experimental crops have been grown in the United States (Nevada and Arizona) and in western provinces of Canada. Sea-buckthorn is also a popular landscaping shrub, valued for its colorful berry clusters that persist through winter. It is used to stabilize riverbanks and steep slopes and is the regional flora of Finland's Satakunta region. Nutrients, Health Effects, and Cosmetics Sea-buckthorn berries are highly nutritious but very acidic and astringent, making them unpleasant to eat raw unless frosted to reduce astringency or mixed with sweeter substances like apple or grape juice. They are used to make pies, jams, juices, lotions, and liquors. When pressed for juice, the resulting liquid separates into three layers: a thick orange cream on top, a middle layer rich in unsaturated fats, and sediment and juice at the bottom. The top two layers are used in cosmetics, while the bottom layer is used for edible products. The berries are rich in antioxidants, which may help inhibit inflammatory disorders, cancer, and other diseases. They contain high levels of vitamin C, carotenoids, vitamin E, amino acids, dietary minerals, β-sitosterol, and polyphenolic acids. Sea-buckthorn has been incorporated into various commercial cosmetic products and nutritional supplements. Its juice remains liquid even at sub-zero temperatures, with a freezing point of −22°C. In India, a factory in Leh produces a multi-vitamin herbal beverage from sea-buckthorn juice for troops in extremely cold regions. Traditional Medicine Sea-buckthorn has been used in traditional medicine for centuries to treat coughs, aid digestion, improve blood circulation, and alleviate pain. In Mongolia, extracts from branches and leaves are used to treat gastrointestinal distress in humans and animals. Bark and leaves are used for diarrhea, gastrointestinal and dermatological disorders, and as topical compresses for rheumatoid arthritis. Flowers may be used as skin softeners. The berries are added to medications for pulmonary, gastrointestinal, cardiac, blood, and metabolic disorders in Indian, Chinese, and Tibetan medicine. They also exhibit potential anticancer activity. Fresh juice, syrup, and oils from the berries or seeds are used for colds, fever, exhaustion, stomach ulcers, cancer, and metabolic disorders. The oil, known as Chharma in some native languages, is used for liver diseases, inflammation, gastrointestinal disorders, eczema, canker sores, wounds, burns, frostbite, psoriasis, lupus erythematosus, and chronic dermatoses. In ophthalmology, berry extracts are used for keratitis, trachoma, eyelid injuries, and conjunctivitis. Organizations The International Center for Research and Training on Seabuckthorn (ICRTS) was established in 1988 by the China Research and Training Center on Seabuckthorn, the Seabuckthorn Office of the Yellow River Water Commission, and the Shaanxi Seabuckthorn Development Office. ICRTS published the research journal Hippophae from 1995 to 2000 but is no longer active. In 2005, an international collaboration called EAN-Seabuck was funded by the European Commission to promote sustainable crop and product development from sea-buckthorn.
